segments.quote: I was going to study something else entirely and then I moved to Port Calder and started noticing that the junction outside my flat behaved differently on different days.
segments.full_text: I was going to study something else entirely and then I moved to Port Calder and started noticing that the junction outside my flat behaved differently on different days. codes.rationale: Acknowledges the influence of personal experience and bias on research direction.

segments.title: System prioritizes vehicle flow over vulnerable pedestrians
segments.quote: The system optimises flow. Flow is measured in vehicles. So when the model has a choice between holding twelve cars and holding one person with a walking frame, the arithmetic is not close.
segments.full_text: The thing I keep coming back to is who gets asked to adapt. The system optimises flow. Flow is measured in vehicles. So when the model has a choice between holding twelve cars and holding one person with a walking frame, the arithmetic is not close. Nobody chose that. It falls out of what got counted.

codes.rationale: Illustrates a deterministic, short-term focus on quantifiable metrics (vehicle flow) without anticipating the consequences for vulnerable users.

segments.title: Warm reception of recommendations does not lead to system change
segments.quote: The group has produced two documents. Both were received warmly. Neither changed a parameter.

segments.title: Department is thoughtful and underfunded, lacking formal mechanisms
segments.quote: They answer emails. I'm not being sarcastic — compared with the vendors, the department is reachable and the people in it are thoughtful and underfunded. The problem isn't that they don't care. It's that caring isn't a mechanism.

summary: This postdoctoral researcher's account reveals a tension between participatory engagement and a lack of systemic responsiveness. The research emerged from a personal frustration, highlighting a deterministic approach to traffic management that prioritizes vehicle flow over vulnerable users. While the researcher actively fosters an inclusive engagement group, the recommendations generated through this process are consistently received positively but fail to translate into tangible system changes. This points to a structural problem: a lack of formal mechanisms for incorporating feedback, leaving the process reliant on the goodwill of individuals. The researcher demonstrates a strong degree of reflexivity, acknowledging the influence of personal bias and critically examining the limitations of current approaches, but struggles to identify a path towards meaningful impact.
transcript:
Interview transcript A02 — Postdoctoral researcher, science and technology studies
Case: Port Calder adaptive traffic signal and pedestrian detection system  |  SYNTHETIC DATA — not a real interview
[Interviewer] How did you come to study this deployment?
[Respondent] I was going to study something else entirely and then I moved to Port Calder and started noticing that the junction outside my flat behaved differently on different days. That's an embarrassing origin story for a research programme but it's the true one. I should say that up front because where a question comes from shapes what you look at, and I was already annoyed before I started.
[Interviewer] What have you found?
[Respondent] The thing I keep coming back to is who gets asked to adapt. The system optimises flow. Flow is measured in vehicles. So when the model has a choice between holding twelve cars and holding one person with a walking frame, the arithmetic is not close. Nobody chose that. It falls out of what got counted.
[Interviewer] Have you worked with residents directly?
[Respondent] Yes, that's most of what I do now. We set up a group with a disability advocacy organisation and a residents' association — eleven people, meeting monthly, and they set the agenda, not me. The first three meetings I talked too much and one of them told me so, which was the most useful supervision I've had.
[Interviewer] Has any of it changed the system?
[Respondent] No. And I want to be careful here because there's a genre of research where the conclusion is 'more participation is needed' and everyone nods and nothing happens. The group has produced two documents. Both were received warmly. Neither changed a parameter. At some point warm reception without change is its own kind of dismissal and I don't yet know what to do about it.
[Interviewer] Is there anything the city does well here?
[Respondent] They answer emails. I'm not being sarcastic — compared with the vendors, the department is reachable and the people in it are thoughtful and underfunded. The problem isn't that they don't care. It's that caring isn't a mechanism. There's no point in the process where what the group says has to be answered in writing before something proceeds. Without that, everything depends on whether the person in post that year happens to be receptive.
